How to read this

AquaWatch maps aquaculture from free satellite imagery, then checks it against the state's own records.

Concept console — real detection at pilot scale, illustrative at statewide scale.

A real detector has run on real (free) Copernicus Sentinel-1 imagery for two belts and validated against hand-labelled ground truth at F1 ≈ 0.74. What is illustrative: the statewide counts, the per-pond registered / unmatched / protected colouring (needs the state registry, not held), the alerts, and the density of tiles drawn. The problem is real and sourced: Andhra has geo-tagged about 2.07 lakh registered ponds, yet in East Godavari alone roughly 18,000 ha of ponds exist on the ground against about 7,000 ha on the books, and one recent drive cleared only 18 of 206 flagged illegal ponds.

In short: the problem is real and sourced, and a real detector has now run on real (free) Copernicus Sentinel-1 imagery for two belts, validated against hand-labelled ground truth at F1 ≈ 0.74. Still illustrative: the statewide counts, the per-pond registered / unmatched / protected colouring (needs the APSADA registry, which we do not hold), the alerts, and the density of tiles the map draws. What is genuine is the geography, ~1,660 OpenStreetMap footprints, and the pilot detection above.

The sweeping imaging pass and the next-pass countdown are illustrative animation, not a live feed. Sentinel-1 revisits this area about every 7 days and imagery is pulled from the archive, not streamed. At 10 m resolution the defensible product is aquaculture extent and blocks, not an exact pond count — dense ponds merge below one pixel.

Why only 1,660? Those are the ponds volunteers have actually drawn in OpenStreetMap — nearly all around Machilipatnam, with the Godavari belts barely covered. Against an estimated quarter-million ponds statewide, that gap is the argument for training a detector rather than relying on crowd-sourced maps.

Scale — and why the map samples

At true density the delta holds well over a hundred thousand ponds, far more than a browser can draw at once. So the map renders roughly one pond in twenty-two as a visual sample, while the counts shown in the panels reflect full scale. A production build would swap this for tiled vector layers.

The three zoom levels

  1. Delta view — a density surface showing where aquaculture pressure concentrates, with a badge per belt.
  2. Belt view — individual ponds resolve into visible tiles, coloured by status.
  3. Pond view — zoom in far enough and every pond becomes clickable, with its own record card.

What the colours mean

  1. Cyan — registered. Lines up with a licensed pond in the state registry. Nothing to do.
  2. Amber — no registry match. Clearly a pond from space, but no licence recorded within 250 m. Likely unregistered.
  3. Red — inside a protected zone. Within the Kolleru sanctuary buffer or coastal regulation zone, where ponds are not permitted at all.

Short version: cyan is fine, amber needs a check, red is a violation.

Controls

Scroll to zoom, drag to pan, click a belt or an individual pond to inspect it. ⛶ hides both side panels, ⤢ returns to the whole delta.
